Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary clinics in Mozambique predominantly use paper-based systems for patient data recording, including handwritten registers, patient-held medical cards, and manual logs later aggregated for national DHIS2 at district levels. No evidence of routine electronic entry at point-of-service in most rural facilities; digital remains limited to pilots and national aggregation. Digital systems: National DHIS2 HMIS for aggregates; pilots like DHIS2 Tracker app for immunization in 5/11 provinces (2024, 19k children); ECR platform developing for facilities; 2024 hospital pilots to reduce paper. Barriers: Rural electricity/connectivity shortages, low digital skills, infrastructure gaps (2025 Digital Health Strategy plans rural pilots with renewables/satellites). Policy ambition (PESS, Digital Strategy) targets EMR/RES by 2030, but rural PoS lags behind—paper default, digital for reporting only. Conservative score 1; pilots hint at 2 potential. (198 words)

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) was supported by five sources describing paper-based data capture with digital limited to pilots/aggregation; those sources were re-verified and remain valid (the Ministry of Health Digital Health Strategy PDF could not be re-fetched directly, returning a 403 error, but its content is corroborated by other sources). Fresh searches identified additional 2024-2025 evidence of expanding facility-level digital pilots: the DHIS2-based Electronic Child Registry (25 facilities, three districts of Maputo province, from May 2024), the MGDH-Birth/e-SiRCEV birth-registration pilot with direct digital data entry by health workers at Chicuque Rural Hospital (Inhambane, from April 2024), and the DISA-SESP HIV laboratory interoperability platform, which by October 2025 covered over 500 health facilities nationwide. These indicate genuine point-of-service digital data capture is now occurring at a meaningful, if still minority, number of rural facilities through programme-specific pilots, beyond mere central aggregation. This warrants an upgrade from 1 (Entirely paper) to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital). Year set to 2025 based on the most recent corroborating sources.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare facilities in Mozambique operate a predominantly paper-based data capture regime, with handwritten registers and patient cards remaining the norm at point of service. Targeted digital pilots nonetheless now reach a meaningful number of facilities: the DHIS2-based Electronic Child Registry captures individual child health records in 25 facilities across three districts of Maputo province (from May 2024); the MGDH-Birth/e-SiRCEV interoperability pilot has health workers at Chicuque Rural Hospital and other Inhambane facilities entering birth data directly into a digital system; and the DISA-SESP laboratory interoperability platform, covering over 500 health facilities nationwide, enables clinicians to receive HIV viral-load results electronically rather than on paper. The Ministry of Health's SIS-RME electronic medical record system is being designed for national roll-out from 2025 but is not yet deployed at rural facility level. Overall, data capture at rural clinics remains mostly paper-based, with pockets of digital capture emerging through disease- and programme-specific pilots.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Mozambique (PRM) use entirely paper-based systems for case files, complaints, and incident reports (e.g., Auto de Notícia forms). A 2014 study of 40 investigators in rural Nampula province found manual information systems in use, with no IT despite staff capability.UFMG Thesis A 2024 example from Rapale district (rural Nampula) shows typed paper-style incident report digitized as PDF.Scribd PRM Form Justice sector digitalization efforts (UNODC seminar 2025) face rural tech access barriers; no police-wide digital case management. Central records manual (fingerprints). Under-resourcing noted.Dullah Omar Score 1: paper-based at station level.

The originally cited sources were re-verified: the UNODC seminar report and the Scribd Auto de Noticia example remain accessible and consistent with the original comments; the UFMG thesis catalogue record could not be re-fetched in usable form (the page returned unrelated content), so this citation could not be independently re-confirmed, though it is consistent with other literature on manual PRM record-keeping. Fresh searches surfaced the InfoViolencia GBV case-recording platform (police-managed, piloted since 2019 in four provinces including rural areas of Gaza, Manica and Nampula) and PGR/SERNIC digitalisation initiatives (GEPROC case management, USAID equipment donations), but these target a narrow case category (gender-based violence) or higher-level institutions (Attorney General's Office, courts) rather than general rural police station record-keeping. No authoritative source indicates general digital case management at rural station level; paper remains the default. Score of 1 confirmed, no change. Year set to 2024, reflecting the most recent evidence describing on-the-ground station practice, medium confidence given the evidence is indicative of continued paper reliance rather than a direct current-year facility survey.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Mozambique (PRM) continue to rely on entirely paper-based systems for case files, complaints and incident reports, such as the handwritten Auto de Notícia form. Studies of rural investigators in Nampula province and recent incident report examples from Rapale district confirm that manual, paper-based recording remains standard practice at station level, with no general digital case management system in place. The InfoViolência platform, a Ministry of Interior/police-managed digital tool for gender-based violence case data, has been piloted since 2019 across four provinces (including rural areas of Gaza, Manica and Nampula) and has trained over 260 officers, but remains in pilot phase rather than routine national deployment and covers a narrow case category rather than general station recording. Broader justice-sector digitalisation efforts, including UNODC-supported seminars and USAID equipment donations to the Attorney General's Office, target higher-level institutions rather than rural station-level data capture. Paper remains the default for day-to-day rural policing records.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Mozambique primarily use paper-based methods for recording administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes. Core EMIS data is collected via hand-filled standardized paper questionnaires during semi-annual school censuses (enrolment in March, results in December), covering student numbers, repeaters, teachers, infrastructure, and resources. These forms are forwarded through districts to provinces for collation and centralized digitization in Maputo—no digital entry at school level. Attendance and marks are tracked in handwritten 'livro de turma' class registers, forming the basis for semester/annual paper school reports on staffing, finances, and pedagogy, which have limited integration with EMIS. No evidence found of routine electronic recording at point-of-service in rural schools. Digital pilots exist, e.g., Carta Escolar (GIS for school mapping/planning, piloted in some provinces but not fully functional or used for attendance/learning data); limited ICT initiatives focus on secondary/urban schools or learning (e.g., SchoolNet, NEPAD e-Schools demos), not admin recording. Key barriers: lack of electricity, computers, internet in rural areas; untrained staff; unreliable infrastructure; focus on basic operations. National EMIS provides aggregate planning data, but rural reality remains paper-dominant, with digitization only at higher levels—wide gap between policy ambitions and rural implementation. revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) was based on three sources describing paper-based EMIS census data collection with centralised digitisation; these were re-checked, though the Scribd EMIS case study could not be re-accessed (client-side captcha) and the World Bank bitstream returned no readable content, so neither could be independently re-confirmed. Fresh searches found an October 2025 Ministry of Education and Culture policy brief confirming that the national EMIS (StatEduc) still depends on physical questionnaires, with a fully digital, real-time entry platform still in development. However, the same and other 2024 sources show that Milange district (Zambézia province, over 300 schools) has scaled EMIS/DHIS2 data capture down to school level since mid-2024, and that DHIS2-based EMIS pilots are underway in Nampula and Zambézia provinces for census data capture. This constitutes genuine, if localised, digital data capture at rural school level, beyond central aggregation, supporting an upgrade from 1 (Entirely paper) to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital). Year set to 2025, based on the most recent authoritative description of national EMIS status.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Mozambique have historically relied on paper-based data collection for the national Education Management Information System (EMIS/StatEduc), with hand-filled questionnaires from the March and December school censuses subsequently digitised at district and national level. The Ministry of Education and Culture confirms that StatEduc still depends on physical questionnaires, with a fully digital, real-time entry platform still in development. However, school-level digital data capture is now emerging in specific districts: Milange district in Zambézia province, with over 300 rural schools, has scaled EMIS/DHIS2 data capture down to the school level since mid-2024, and pilots using the DHIS2 platform are under way in Nampula and Zambézia provinces for statistical census data capture. Attendance and marks (livro de turma) generally remain in handwritten class registers. The overall picture is of a mostly paper-based system with an emerging, still localised, layer of digital data capture at rural school level.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural civil registration posts (345 administrative posts) predominantly use paper forms for recording births, which are then transmitted (via mobile notifications or electronic media) to district conservatories for digitization in the eCRVS system.UNECA CRVS Snapshot Local agents fill forms at point-of-service; districts enter electronically, with data synced centrally.CRVS Webinar Mozambique Digital systems rolled out to all 68 conservatories and ~120 posts (2018, no rural split), plus 156 hospital posts (2024) and experimental offline modules for conflict zones.Child Identity Presentation Under-5 birth registration at 32% (2023 DHS), indicating gaps. Barriers: poor rural internet/electricity, conflict/cyclones damaging infrastructure, low capacity/training.World Bank Blog National SIRCEV plan (2019-29) targets 80%, with donor pilots (UNICEF/WB), but rural point-of-care remains paper-default with digital aggregation.

revision_notes: Original score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) was supported by three sources describing paper-based registration at rural posts with district-level digitisation; these were re-verified (the UNECA snapshot and CRVS webinar PDFs re-fetched successfully; the Child Identity presentation was not re-fetched but is corroborated by other sources) and remain accurate. Fresh searches confirmed and updated this picture: the e-SiRCEV electronic civil registration system is confirmed integrated with national ID and health systems (crvslaws.org, updated May 2025), and a 2024 pilot (Jembi/Saudigitus, funded by Vital Strategies/Bloomberg Philanthropies) has enabled real-time digital birth data entry at rural facilities including Chicuque Rural Hospital, expanding from 5 to 19 participating health facilities and registering over 11,500 births by 2025. A separate 'E-Registo, E-xisto!' initiative established 48 secondary registration offices in health centres across Maputo, Gaza and Nampula provinces for digital registration of children aged 0-5 months. Under-5 birth registration completeness nevertheless remains around 31-32% (2022-23 DHS), confirming that paper remains the norm outside these donor-supported pilot sites. Score of 2 confirmed, no change. Year set to 2024, based on the concrete pilot milestones and interoperability launch, high confidence.
revised_comments: Rural civil registration posts in Mozambique predominantly use paper forms to record births and other vital events, which are transmitted to district conservatories for entry into the electronic civil registration system (e-SiRCEV), established under the 2018-revised Civil Registration Code and integrated with national ID and health systems. Since 2024, a digital interoperability pilot between the Hospital Data Management System (MGDH-Birth) and e-SiRCEV has enabled health workers at rural facilities, including Chicuque Rural Hospital in Inhambane province, to enter birth data directly into a digital system with instant confirmation in the civil registry, expanding from five to nineteen participating facilities and registering over 11,500 births. A separate initiative, 'E-Registo, E-xisto!', established 48 secondary registration offices in health centres across Maputo, Gaza and Nampula provinces to digitally register children aged 0-5 months. Despite these advances, under-five birth registration completeness remains low, at around 31-32% (2022-23 Demographic and Health Survey), reflecting that most rural point-of-service registration still occurs on paper, with digital capture concentrated in donor-supported pilot sites rather than nationwide.
